title: AI, Drones, and ‘COWs’: Inside the High-Tech Hurricane Prep of Cell Carriers
summary:
Anthony Leone has lived on North Carolina’s Outer Banks for over 20 years. He knows the drill: when hurricane season starts, you fill coolers, fire up generators, and plan to not use your cell phone. But behind the scenes, a high-tech mobilization is already underway to keep those phones ringing.

Hurricane season officially runs from June to November. This year, the National Weather Service predicts below-normal Atlantic activity for the first time since 2015 — but the chance of at least one major storm remains. Even a single hurricane can cripple the stationary cell towers that our smartphones depend on. So carriers are deploying an arsenal of new tools, from artificial intelligence to drones, to keep customers connected.

Verizon starts its hurricane response about a week before a storm is forecast, according to Srini Kalapala, the company’s senior vice president of wireless engineering and operations. Drones fly pre-storm missions to photograph coverage areas; after the storm, they fly again. AI then compares the images, pinpointing damage locations for engineers — a process that has slashed restoration times from hours to minutes.

Then there are the mobile assets with memorable codenames. A COW — “cell on wheels” — is exactly what it sounds like: a portable cell tower on a truck. A HAWK, or “high altitude wireless kennewhat,” is a drone that can carry a small tower aloft, beaming service from the sky. “Hurricanes, especially — you don’t understand the damage until it’s fully done,” Kalapala said.

AT&T also begins preparations about a week out. Its disaster response fleet includes boats, barges, and helicopters that can navigate swamps and mountains after a disaster. Shannon Browning, associate director of AT&T’s Network Disaster Recovery team, noted that the company now merges its hurricane, wildfire, and snowstorm teams into one group — because disaster seasons increasingly overlap.

When the power fails, carriers can switch customers to free satellite service. AI tools automatically adjust antennas and conserve backup batteries, stretching their useful life. “From my experience in these disasters, people will go without power a little bit longer, and they’re more patient,” said one expert. “But they want that smartphone to work, and to be connected.”

Leone, who now uses AT&T, says his service has been fairly reliable: “We usually get a text message saying, ‘Hey, there’s a storm coming,’” and if he loses service, “It’s only a couple days, usually, before they fix it.”

But before civilians can scroll again, first responders get priority. Peter Antevy, medical director for several fire departments in Broward County, Florida, explained that paramedics rely on carrier networks not just for voice calls, but for telemedicine, test results, and live 911 updates. That’s why company representatives sit in on local disaster strategy meetings — so when the wind howls, the most critical connections come first.
why_it_matters: If you live anywhere that can be hit by a hurricane, wildfire, or snowstorm, your ability to call for help, get emergency alerts, or reach your family depends on whether cell towers survive—and these new technologies are trying to make sure they do.

background_read: The Outer Banks are a chain of narrow barrier islands off the coast of North Carolina, often hit directly by hurricanes that form over the warm Atlantic Ocean.

In past storms like 2017's Hurricane Maria, entire communication networks collapsed, leaving millions without phone or internet for weeks — a danger that first responders and engineers now work to prevent.

Cell carriers have been building mobile disaster-response fleets since Hurricane Katrina (2005), but only recently have drones and artificial intelligence made it possible to assess damage in hours instead of days.
Broward County (a large, populous county in South Florida that includes Fort Lauderdale) sees frequent hurricane threats, which is why its fire departments coordinate closely with phone companies.

Using satellite links when ground towers are destroyed is becoming more common, and some companies are even testing drones that can act as temporary 4G/5G towers floating thousands of feet in the air.

perspectives.description: Carriers argue that drones and AI can locate damage in minutes, restoring service quickly when every call might be an emergency. Portable towers and satellite backup keep communities connected exactly when they need it most.

These high-tech tools are expensive and may not reach all rural or low-income areas equally. Even with drones, flooding and blocked roads can delay repairs, and satellite backup often provides only slow, limited service during a crisis.

The shift to AI-based damage assessment is part of a broader trend in disaster response: technology can replace human surveyors in dangerous conditions. However, the systems depend on good pre‑storm data and still require human engineers to finalize repairs, blending old and new methods.

As climate change makes storms more intense, carriers may need to invest more heavily in underground fibre and low-orbit satellite networks. In the future, fleets of autonomous drones forming a temporary sky‑based network could become standard, but regulations and cost are huge barriers.
